public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1093

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1093](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1093)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos1093

open Finset Nat

/--
If defined, the deficiency is the count of $0 \le i < k$ such that $n - i$ is $k$-smooth,
that is, divisible only by primes $\le k$.

`Nat.smoothNumbers m` is the set of positive naturals all of whose prime factors are
$< m$, so "$k$-smooth" in the sense above is `Nat.smoothNumbers (k + 1)`.
-/
noncomputable def deficiency (n k : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  #{i ∈ range k | n - i ∈ smoothNumbers (k + 1)}

/--
Are there infinitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency 1?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_1093.parts.i :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {x : ℕ × ℕ | let k := x.1; let n := x.2; 2 * k ≤ n ∧ deficiency n k = 1 ∧
      ∀ p, p.Prime → (p ∣ choose n k) → k < p}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Are there only finitely many binomial coefficients with deficiency > 1?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem erdos_1093.parts.ii :
    {x : ℕ × ℕ | let k := x.1; let n := x.2; 2 * k ≤ n ∧ deficiency n k > 1 ∧
      ∀ p, p.Prime → (p ∣ choose n k) → k < p}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos1093

reformulations.difference: The source defines deficiency only on its admissible domain, whereas the Lean helper returns a natural-number count for every n and k.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Both theorems explicitly impose n ≥ 2k and exclude every prime divisor ≤ k of the binomial coefficient. On that domain, membership in smoothNumbers (k + 1) is exactly the source's condition that every prime divisor is ≤ k. Values outside the source's domain cannot enter either theorem. In the scratch file, an independently stated Option-valued partial definition was proved equivalent to the file's domain conditions together with deficiency n k = d.

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement counts eligible (k,n) pairs. This also agrees with interpreting the source as counting distinct numerical binomial-coefficient values.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Positive deficiency excludes k = 0. For 1 ≤ k and 2k ≤ n, n ≤ Nat.choose n k. Consequently, the pairs yielding any fixed coefficient value b satisfy k ≤ n ≤ b, so every fiber is finite. Infinitely many eligible pairs therefore exist exactly when infinitely many distinct eligible coefficient values exist. This equivalence was proved in Lean and instantiated for the exact set in part i.

reformulations.difference: Finiteness is expressed for eligible (k,n) pairs rather than a set of numerical coefficient values.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: As in part i, positive deficiency and 2k ≤ n imply 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ Nat.choose n k. The coefficient-value map thus has finite fibers on the eligible set. Its image is finite if and only if the pair set is finite. This equivalence was proved in Lean and instantiated for the exact set in part ii.
